passage: "Irfan, you haven't touched your roti." "Not hungry, Pooja apa." "Since when? What happened?" "Mr Verma. In Maths. I got the answer wrong and he said, in front of everybody, 'Sit down, you're useless, you'll never amount to anything.' Everyone laughed." "And what did you do?" "Nothing. My face was burning. I wanted to shout at him. I just sat there and stared at the desk." "That took strength, you know." "It doesn't feel like it. I feel stupid." "A wrong answer is a wrong answer. What he said was about him, not you. Tell Abbu tonight." "He'll say don't make trouble." "He'll listen. And if it happens again, we go to the vice principal, together." Irfan picked up the roti at last. 🤍

qa.q: What did Mr Verma say to Irfan in front of the class?
qa.a: "Sit down, you're useless, you'll never amount to anything."

qa.q: What was Irfan feeling in the classroom, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Shame and rage. His face was burning and he wanted to shout at the teacher, but he sat there staring at the desk.

qa.q: What would you advise Irfan to do next?
qa.a: Tell Abbu tonight, remember the insult says something about the teacher's conduct and not his worth, and report it to the vice principal if it repeats. 🤍

qa.q: How does Pooja see what happened in the classroom?
qa.a: She sees Irfan's silence as strength, not weakness. She thinks the words reflect on the teacher, and she wants to stand with him if it happens again.

grounding: A teenager humiliated by a teacher stays composed, tells a family member and plans to report if it repeats.

passage:
Tuesday. In the middle of maths, Mr Rao held up Kashish's notebook and said, "Look at this. Even a Class 3 child writes better. Are you stupid or just lazy?" The class laughed. Kashish's face burned; her fists clenched under the desk. She wanted to shout back. She kept her mouth shut and stared at the board until the bell.
That evening she told Mummy everything, crying. Mummy listened, hugged her and said, "That was not okay. It says nothing about you." She wrote down exactly what was said, with the date, and emailed the school coordinator that night.
Thursday. Mummy and Kashish met the coordinator, Mrs Mathew, before school. Mrs Mathew listened carefully. "Thank you for telling us. No teacher should speak to a student like that. I'll speak to Mr Rao today."
Monday. Mr Rao returned the notebook without a word. Kashish's friend Devika whispered, "If he does it again, we'll both write it down."

qa.q: What did Mr Rao hold up in front of the class?
How did Kashish feel when the class laughed?
qa.a: She felt humiliated and furious, face burning and fists clenched, but she kept her composure.

qa.q: Which steps helped Kashish, and why?
qa.a: Staying calm, telling Mummy that evening, writing down the details and meeting the coordinator made sure adults dealt with it.

qa.q: How does Mrs Mathew see the incident?
qa.a: She sees it as unacceptable behaviour from a teacher and promises to speak to Mr Rao that day.

grounding: A teen insulted by a teacher in front of the class keeps composure, tells a parent and reports it through the coordinator.

passage:
Santosh beta, you came home red-eyed because your teacher mocked you. Come, sit with your Dilnaz Aunty. Let me tell you about my science teacher.
In Class 10, Mrs Kapoor called me to the board and, when I got the formula wrong, said to the whole class, "This is what happens when girls think they can do science." Everyone laughed. I wanted to throw the chalk at her. Instead I put it down very carefully and walked back to my seat. My legs were shaking.
That evening I told my father. He was very quiet, then he said, "She is wrong about you." The turning point was the next morning: he went with me to the headmaster and repeated her words exactly as I had written them down.
The headmaster spoke to her. When she did it again a month later, we reported it again.
I became a chemistry teacher, Santosh. And I have never once mocked a child.

qa.q: What did Mrs Kapoor say to the class?
qa.a: "This is what happens when girls think they can do science."

qa.q: How did young Dilnaz feel when the class laughed?
qa.a: She felt humiliated and furious, wanting to throw the chalk, and her legs shook as she walked back.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Her father went with her to the headmaster the next morning with her written record, and they reported it again when it happened again.

qa.q: How might young Dilnaz's father have felt hearing the story?
qa.a: He likely felt angry and protective, quiet at first but determined to show her the teacher was wrong.

grounding: An elder recalls being insulted by a teacher, keeping her composure, telling a parent and reporting it when it repeated.
